title: Contract Intelligence: A Scaled Benchmark for Measuring Contract Understanding
author: Harvey Team

dom.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source accepts the need for realistic, task-specific evaluation and materially extends it with a contract-focused benchmark comparing extraction accuracy against human experts across more than 4,000 data points. It also distinguishes simple verbatim retrieval from higher-value reasoning and synthesis, reinforcing the cluster’s view that broad scores should not be treated as complete professional competence.
qs: Today, we're publishing initial findings from our Contract Intelligence benchmark, which encompasses more than 4,000 data points aimed at measuring extraction accuracy on varying contract types and terms and comparing that accuracy to human experts.
When we discuss contract use cases with clients, they also indicate a clear need to have models reason, understand, or synthesize those data points to create higher-value structured data.

kp.k: Contract intelligence extends beyond verbatim extraction
kp.d: Harvey reports that clients want models to reason about and synthesize contract terms into higher-value structured data. Its benchmark distinguishes extraction of verbatim information, single-term review requiring interpretation, and multi-term understanding connecting disparate provisions. These are presented as distinct levels of contract understanding rather than a single extraction task.
qs: When we discuss contract use cases with clients, they also indicate a clear need to have models reason, understand, or synthesize those data points to create higher-value structured data.
Each of these types of questions examines a different layer of understanding, from straightforward identification to conceptual reasoning across multiple terms.

kp.k: Initial benchmark compares models and attorneys across 4,000-plus datapoints
kp.d: In its 21 November 2025 publication, Harvey reports initial findings from more than 4,000 data points comparing contract extraction accuracy with human experts. Internal lawyers and customers helped select contract types and key data points, ranging from 22 for Side Letters to 37 for LPAs. Questions were closed-ended and expressed in natural language, with contracts selected for diversity of format and term expression. Harvey explicitly characterizes the publication as selected outcomes rather than complete results.
qs: Today, we're publishing initial findings from our Contract Intelligence benchmark, which encompasses more than 4,000 data points aimed at measuring extraction accuracy on varying contract types and terms and comparing that accuracy to human experts.
This publication highlights key outcomes and does not purport to include every result.
The number of data points varied depending on contract complexity, ranging from 22 (Side Letters) to 37 (LPAs) data points for a contract type.

kp.k: Harvey researchers adjudicate human-model disagreements and maintain ground truth
kp.d: Contracted transactional attorneys and Review tables answered the same contract questions. Harvey's Applied Legal Researchers with relevant transactional backgrounds resolved disagreements and sampled agreements to detect shared misunderstanding, producing ground truth and scores for humans and models. Future Vault evaluations use this baseline automatically, while researchers sample both agreements and disagreements to check its continued validity. Harvey reports adding, reviewing and evaluating thousands of data points monthly.
qs: Disagreements in responses were resolved by Applied Legal Researchers (ALRs) at Harvey with relevant transactional backgrounds.
Data points where models and humans agree were also sampled to ensure that agreement didn't cover up misunderstanding.
This ground truth baseline is then used to automatically evaluate future Vault systems for accuracy.
In this way, thousands of data points are added, reviewed, and evaluated monthly, making it one of the largest (and constantly growing) sets of annotated contract data anywhere.

kp.k: Specialized models perform competitively; generic models struggle
kp.d: Harvey reports that out-of-the-box LLMs identified around 65–70% of valid deal points, whereas domain-specialized models performed competitively with humans on the benchmark's contract review and structured analytical-data task. It qualifies the reported overall-score equivalence by stressing that humans and models do not perform the task in the same way.
qs: Out-of-the-box LLMs struggled on [contract extraction], only identifying around 65-70% of valid deal points.
When domain-specialized, LLMs can perform competitively with humans at reviewing contracts and producing structured, analytical data
This observed equivalence in overall scores does not, however, mean that humans and models perform the task the same way.

kp.k: Lawyer-model collaboration achieves the highest reported scores
kp.d: Harvey reports that lawyers using Review tables in Vault achieved the benchmark's best performance, routinely outscoring either lawyers or LLMs alone by 5% or more, depending on baseline contract complexity. The finding concerns combined human-model performance on contract understanding and analysis, which Harvey interprets as evidence of complementary capabilities.
qs: In digging into the results, we've found that the best performance on our Contract Intelligence benchmark came from lawyers working with Review tables in Vault.
outscored either the lawyer or LLM alone by 5% or more
Model and human intelligence are complementary on issues of contract understanding and analysis

kp.k: Models overreach beyond documents and overinterpret consent requirements
kp.d: Harvey identifies two recurring model failure patterns. Models sometimes made reasonable but unconfirmable claims about main agreements incorporated by reference into Side Letters, whereas humans recognized missing information. Models also gave overly literal answers, such as treating a consent requirement as both consent and notice because notice precedes consent; lawyers instead identified consent as the operative requirement.
qs: First, they could be overeager, making assumptions about information beyond the four corners of the provided contract.
Humans, by contrast, recognized the limits of what was in front of them and noted the absence of that information.
Second, we saw that LLMs can overthink, producing technically correct but overly literal responses to questions.
Lawyers, on the other hand, collapsed this information hierarchy and correctly noted that the contract simply required consent.

kp.k: Human errors are less predictable than model failure patterns
kp.d: Harvey reports that consistent judgment errors were rare among highly skilled experts, while human mistakes more often involved isolated lapses, such as reversing buyer and seller or missing a decisive phrase. On its dataset, Harvey says models did not exhibit this type of failure: once a model understood a data point's core concepts, it routinely earned full credit across varying contract types. The claim is expressly limited to the observed dataset.
qs: Although there are some consistent errors of judgment, these tend to be rare amongst high skill experts.

More common are errors that come from just being human: accidental transpositions of buyer and seller, missing a key phrase that changes the meaning of a provision, and other one-off mistakes that don't recur through the lawyer's work.

Notably, models do not exhibit this sort of failure on our dataset — where a model understands the core concepts reflected in a datapoint it routinely scores full credit across varying contract types.

kp.k: Planned expansion targets complexity and drafting-sensitive performance
kp.d: Harvey plans to expand the benchmark along three axes: contract types, contracts per type and deal points. It specifically proposes adding complex Merger and Credit Agreements, more examples within existing types because model performance varies with drafting, and deal points presenting novel model challenges or customer value. These are ongoing development plans, not reported results from the expanded benchmark.
qs: Work on our Contract Intelligence benchmark is ongoing, and we're committed to continuously deepening it across the three key axes on which we measure intelligence: contract type, number of contracts, and deal points.
We will add new contract types with a particular emphasis on complex contracts like Merger and Credit Agreements.
We'll also add additional contracts to each set — even contracts of the same type can be diverse, and we've seen varied model performance depending on how key terms are drafted and expressed.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey Team claims that domain-specialized LLMs can match lawyers on benchmarked contract-analysis tasks, while lawyers using Harvey's Review tables outperform either lawyers or LLMs alone by 5% or more.
pts.d: The source reports current benchmark findings rather than predictions of profession-wide change. It claims that specialized models can produce structured, analytical contract data competitively with human experts, and that combining lawyer and model intelligence produces the best results. The reported improvement is described as '5% or more'; the publication does not specify whether this means percentage points or relative improvement. Harvey attributes complementarity to different error patterns: models make unsupported assumptions about material outside the supplied contract or give overly literal answers, whereas lawyers make occasional transpositions and overlook decisive phrases. Harvey says models did not exhibit the latter kind of error on its dataset once they understood the relevant concepts. It also reports that out-of-the-box LLMs identified only around 65–70% of valid deal points. These are claims about contract understanding and answer accuracy, not measured time savings, workforce displacement, or market-wide effects.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Harvey's own Contract Intelligence benchmark, comprising more than 4,000 data points and comparisons with contracted transactional attorneys.
pts.d: Harvey says internal lawyers and customers helped select valuable contract types and deal points. Closed-ended natural-language questions cover verbatim extraction, single-term interpretation, and reasoning across multiple terms, with 22 to 37 data points per contract type. Contracted transactional attorneys and Review tables answered the questions; Harvey Applied Legal Researchers with transactional backgrounds resolved disagreements and sampled agreements to establish ground truth. The publication reports combined lawyer-and-tool performance, but does not separately describe the procedure used to test that combined condition or provide complete results. Its explanations of complementarity draw on observed error patterns, including assumptions about agreements incorporated by reference, overly literal treatment of consent and notice, and human transpositions or missed phrases. This is a vendor-authored benchmark, not an independently attributed evaluation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern initial findings published on 21 November 2025, conditional on domain specialization, the tested tasks and contracts, and contract complexity.
pts.d: Harvey limits human-competitive performance to domain-specialized LLMs on this specific contract-review task. The size of the combined lawyer-and-tool advantage depends on baseline contract complexity, and equivalent overall scores do not imply equivalent reasoning or error patterns. The observation that models avoid certain human mistakes is expressly restricted to the dataset and to deal points whose core concepts the model understands. Harvey also reports performance variation with drafting and expression of terms. It describes ongoing monthly benchmark growth and plans to add contract types, contracts, and deal points, especially complex Merger and Credit Agreements, without giving a completion date or forecasting when broader capabilities will be achieved.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected users are attorneys reviewing contracts, particularly transactional lawyers using Review tables in Harvey Vault, and customers seeking structured contract analysis.
pts.d: The claimed benefit is improved accuracy when lawyers work with Review tables and the ability to obtain higher-value structured information requiring interpretation rather than verbatim extraction alone. The source frames the product as supporting attorneys and presents lawyer-plus-tool use as the strongest arrangement; it does not claim that lawyers can be removed from the workflow. Contracted transactional attorneys serve as human comparators, while Harvey Applied Legal Researchers establish and maintain benchmark ground truth. Customers help identify useful contract types and deal points. The publication does not distinguish benefits by law-firm size, in-house versus outside counsel, or client market segment, and makes no concrete claims about fees, employment, or access to justice.
